Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On August 30, 2023, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) issued its second estimate for the U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP) for the second quarter of 2023. The report indicated that the U.S. economy expanded at a solid 2.1% annualized rate. This figure, however, was a downward revision from the advance estimate of 2.4%. According to the BEA, the update primarily reflected downward revisions to private inventory investment and nonresidential fixed investment. The overall increase in real GDP was driven by gains in consumer spending, nonresidential fixed investment, and spending by state, local, and federal governments. This release provided a more comprehensive view of the economy's performance leading into the third quarter, influencing market perceptions of economic strength and the future of the USD. <2> The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics announced that the Producer Price Index (PPI) for final demand saw a seasonally adjusted increase of 0.3% in July 2023. This rise was primarily driven by a 0.5% increase in the index for final demand services, which represents the most significant advance in this category since August 2022. The data for the 12 months ending in July showed an unadjusted increase of 0.8% for the final demand index. <3> On August 4, 2023, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 187,000 in July, a figure below the average monthly gain of 312,000 over the prior 12 months and under economists' expectations. [1] The unemployment rate ticked down to 3.5%, continuing a trend of remaining under 4% for an extended period. [1, 3] Key job gains occurred in sectors such as health care, social assistance, and financial activities. [1, 3] The report was interpreted as a sign of a cooling but still resilient labor market, which could influence future interest rate decisions by the Federal Reserve and consequently affect financial markets, including the USD/BRL exchange rate. <4> The Bureau of Labor Statistics announced on July 12, 2023, that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) for all urban consumers rose 3.0 percent over the 12-month period ending in June 2023, before seasonal adjustment. [2, 3] This marked the smallest 12-month increase since the period ending in March 2021. [2, 3] The data indicated a significant deceleration in inflation from its peak of 9.1 percent in June 2022. On a monthly basis, the CPI increased by 0.2 percent in June on a seasonally adjusted basis. [2, 3] The shelter index was the largest contributor to this monthly increase, accounting for over 70 percent of the rise. [2] <5> In its 254th meeting on June 21, 2023, the Monetary Policy Committee (Copom) of the Banco Central do Brasil unanimously decided to maintain the benchmark Selic interest rate at 13.75% per year. This marked the seventh consecutive time the rate was held at this level. The committee's decision was based on the global economic outlook, which remained challenging, and a domestic scenario showing gradual deceleration of economic activity. While consumer inflation had shown some reduction, underlying inflation measures were still above the target range. The Copom stated that the disinflationary process tended to be slower and that de-anchored inflation expectations required caution and parsimony, justifying the strategy of maintaining the Selic rate for an extended period to ensure inflation converges toward the target. At the time, inflation projections for 2023 and 2024 stood at 5.0% and 3.4%, respectively. <6> The U.S. Census Bureau announced that advance estimates for retail and food services sales for May 2023 were $686.6 billion, a 0.3% increase from the previous month. This followed a 0.4% increase in April, marking the second consecutive monthly gain and suggesting consumer spending remained resilient despite economic headwinds. Categories showing notable increases included building materials at 2.2% and motor vehicles and parts at 1.4%. Core retail sales, which are used to calculate GDP, saw a 0.2% rise. While nominal sales showed growth, when adjusted for inflation, real retail sales were estimated to have risen by 0.2%. <7> The U.S. goods and services trade deficit increased to $74.6 billion in April 2023, a significant rise of $14.0 billion from the revised March figure of $60.6 billion. [1, 2] This widening gap was a result of a $9.2 billion decrease in exports to $249.0 billion and a $4.8 billion increase in imports to $323.6 billion, which may suggest a slowdown in global demand for U.S. products. [1, 2] <8> The Conference Board announced its Consumer Confidence Index dropped to 102.3 in May 2023, a decrease from April's upwardly revised figure of 103.7, marking the fourth decline in five months. This fall was attributed to a more pessimistic outlook from consumers, particularly those over 55, regarding current business and labor market conditions, alongside persistent concerns about inflation. The Present Situation Index, which reflects consumers' views on current conditions, fell from 151.8 to 148.6. Similarly, the Expectations Index, a measure of the six-month outlook for income, business, and labor, edged down from 71.7 to 71.5. This Expectations Index has remained below the 80-point threshold, a level often indicating a potential recession within the next year, for every month since February 2022, with only one exception. <9> The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) released its second estimate for the first-quarter 2023 Gross Domestic Product (GDP), revealing an upward revision in the annualized growth rate to 1.3%. This was an increase from the 1.1% reported in the advance estimate. The primary driver for this revision was an upward adjustment to private inventory investment.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The release of weaker-than-expected Brazilian Gross Domestic Product (GDP) data for the third quarter of 2025 altered behavioral sentiment among currency traders. Expanding by just 0.1% in the three months to September 2025, the growth missed market expectations of a 0.2% expansion as private consumption stalled. This lackluster economic performance consolidated an ongoing slowdown in the Brazilian economy, fueling speculation of imminent interest rate cuts by the Central Bank of Brazil and causing the Brazilian Real to depreciate while the USD/BRL pair surged. <2> On November 12, 2025, the U.S. House of Representatives passed a critical continuing resolution (voting 222-209) to fund the government. This pivotal spending bill acted as a major catalyst for the USD/BRL currency pair. As markets anticipated the resolution of the U.S. government shutdown, a wave of risk appetite was triggered, adding downward pressure on the U.S. Dollar relative to the Brazilian Real. <3> Following an investigation by the U.S. Department of Commerce, which announced its final affirmative antidumping and countervailing duty determinations on August 26, 2025, the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) made a subsequent final determination. As reported on November 11, 2025, the USITC concluded that the U.S. steel industry has been materially injured by imports of corrosion-resistant steel products. This affirmative injury finding applies to imports from Australia, Brazil, Canada, Mexico, the Netherlands, South Africa, Taiwan, the Republic of Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, and Vietnam. The USITC's vote was the final step required for the Department of Commerce to issue antidumping and countervailing duty orders on these imports. <4> On November 12, 2025, BNP Paribas Wealth Management published its 'Currencies Focus - November 2025' report. The analysis, featuring insights from Deputy Global CIO Guy Ertz, details the dynamics between the U.S. Dollar and the Brazilian Real. The report emphasizes that the U.S. Federal Reserve's ongoing rate cut cycle, when contrasted against the Central Bank of Brazil's hawkish stance, sustains a highly supportive interest rate differential for the Brazilian Real. <5> In late October 2025, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires in Brazil, Gabriel Escobar, met with Brazilian mining executives to discuss a strategic partnership focused on the rare earth and critical minerals sector. The meetings, which took place during an industry event in Salvador, Bahia, were part of a broader U.S. strategy to diversify critical mineral supply chains and reduce dependency on China, which controls approximately 90% of global rare earth processing. The discussions aimed to establish a bilateral cooperation framework that includes technology transfer for advanced processing, joint research into sustainable extraction, and knowledge sharing on environmental and safety protocols. This positions Brazil, with the world's second-largest documented rare earth reserves at 21 million tons, as a key potential partner for the United States. The talks are also linked to ongoing, broader trade negotiations concerning U.S. tariffs on Brazilian goods. <6> The U.S. Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announced a 25 basis point interest rate cut at its October 28-29, 2025, meeting. This decision lowered the federal funds target rate to a range of 3.75% to 4.00%. This was the second consecutive rate cut, following a similar reduction in September 2025. The committee's official statement was released on October 29, 2025, noting that the move was made in light of increasing downside risks to employment. The vote was not unanimous, with two members dissenting from the majority decision. The committee also announced it would conclude the reduction of its aggregate securities holdings on December 1, 2025. <7> On October 29, 2025, the U.S. Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) announced a 25 basis point interest rate cut, lowering the target range for the federal funds rate to 3.75% to 4.00%. This widely anticipated decision marked the second consecutive rate cut. The announcement came after a two-day policy meeting and was made amidst concerns about rising layoffs and a government shutdown that delayed the release of key economic data. The FOMC statement noted that while economic activity was expanding at a moderate pace, job gains had slowed and inflation remained somewhat elevated. The vote was not unanimous, with a 10-2 majority. One member preferred a larger 50-basis-point cut, while another favored no change to the rate. <8> The Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) implemented its second consecutive interest rate cut on October 29, 2025, lowering the benchmark federal funds rate by 25 basis points to a target range of 3.75% to 4.00%. This decision, made during the October 28-29 meeting, was widely anticipated and aimed to support slowing economic growth amid concerns about the labor market. The move followed a similar rate cut in September. The vote was not unanimous, with two members dissenting from the majority decision. News of the rate cut was published by multiple outlets on October 29 and October 30, 2025. <9> The U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) published its Monthly Energy Review (MER) for October on October 28, 2025. This primary report provides comprehensive and historical U.S. energy statistics, including data on total energy production, consumption, trade, and prices. The MER is a key indicator of energy market trends that can significantly affect inflation and the broader economy. By its nature, the report details statistics from previous months, with the data being preliminary and subject to revision. The October 2025 edition included revisions to uranium statistics in coordination with the 2024 Uranium Marketing Annual Report. <10> Following a meeting on the sidelines of the 47th ASEAN Summit in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, on October 26, 2025, U.S. President Donald Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva announced that their teams would immediately begin negotiations to resolve U.S. tariffs on Brazilian goods. The discussions are aimed at addressing the 50% tariffs the U.S. had imposed on most Brazilian exports. Described as a significant diplomatic step, the announcement signals a potential easing of trade tensions that have impacted bilateral economic relations. President Lula characterized the meeting as "surprisingly good" and "great," expressing confidence that a solution could be found within days. President Trump also conveyed optimism, stating he believed they could make "some pretty good deals for both countries." Brazil's Foreign Minister, Mauro Vieira, echoed this positive sentiment, calling the talks "very positive and productive."
